title: Ang 219–220: Guru Tegh Bahadur
hook: the ninth Guru's Gauri hymns on pride and the passing world
tomorrow: how do you steer a mind as stubborn as an elephant?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ang 200: trust. Seed, soil, water, wait, and an open palm. Today, the ninth Guru, on what other people say about you.

A clip of you lands in the group chat. Simran's was eight seconds long: her dad's truck, a row of orange cones, one cone going down. Maya posted it with a crying-laughing face, and the replies poured in. Two days earlier, the same chat had called her a legend for one clean parallel park. Same people, same week. The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, has two short pages in Gauri, and they speak straight into that chat.
screen: `EIGHT SECONDS, ONE CONE.` → `LEGEND ON TUESDAY.` → `MEME BY THURSDAY.`

segments.voice: On Ang 219 he says, in paraphrase: O holy ones, give up the pride of the mind. Then he paints the person who's free of it: one who takes pleasure and pain alike, and honor and dishonor too; who stays beyond both delight and grief; who lets go of praise and slander both. That one, he says, has grasped the essence of the world. Pride, here, isn't only bragging. It's needing the chat to say legend. It's the sting when it says lol. Both come from the same place: a self waiting to be scored. In another hymn on the same page, he turns to how strange the world is: one thing perishes, while someone else believes he'll last forever, and the wonder of it can't be grasped. A clip that felt huge on Tuesday is gone by Friday. So what does the ninth Guru give you for a week like this? Not a thicker skin. A wider view. Praise and mockery are weather; they pass over. What doesn't pass is the One his hymns keep pointing to. Holding praise and insult alike isn't coldness. It's the freedom to laugh at the cone, too.
screen: `GIVE UP THE PRIDE OF THE MIND.` · `PRAISE AND INSULT, HELD ALIKE.` · `ONE PERISHES, ONE THINKS IT LASTS.` · `NOT A THICKER SKIN: A WIDER VIEW.` · then, large: `THE NINTH GURU.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write the last kind thing someone said about you on one side, and the last thing that stung on the other. Hold it, and notice it's one piece of paper, light either way. Set it down, and breathe as if neither side were face up.
Ang 219: where Guru Tegh Bahadur's Gauri hymns begin. Give up the mind's pride; hold praise and insult alike.
Your line: the ninth guru. Praise and insult are both weather, and weather passes. Catch you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1475 COUNTS.` → `GAURI · 6 OF 17.` → `TOMORROW: HOW DO YOU STEER A MIND AS STUBBORN AS AN ELEPHANT?`

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, headed Mahala 9, are sung as kirtan and read in the Granth's order; Sikhs remember him as the ninth Guru, and his lines on holding praise and insult alike picture a steady mind.

fork.setup: your coworker is publicly thanked by the boss on Monday and criticized on Thursday, and can't sleep either night. what does Ang 219 offer?
options: both nights come from one place: a self waiting to be scored.
keep Monday's praise close; it cancels out Thursday's insult.
stop caring about work at all; the world is passing anyway.
fork.reveal: the ninth Guru asks for praise and slander both let go, honor and dishonor held alike. not coldness: freedom from the scoreboard.

original.note: Gurmukhi: maan, pride or honor; Ang 219 asks for the mind's pride to be given up.

notes: v3 storyline (days 1471–1484): Simran is learning to drive in the yard of her dad Harjit's trucking company, with the test at the end of the second week. Bebe Jaswant appears once a week (1474, 1480); Maya, her best friend, comes in and out; paced over two weeks, no overnight turnarounds. Day 1475: Maya posts a clip of Simran knocking over a cone; two days earlier the chat praised her.
